analysis.one_liner: Requires employers to pay time-and-a-half to hourly workers who work on federal holidays.
analysis.headline: Introduced in February 2026 by a single senator with no cosponsors, it sits in the Senate labor committee with no vote scheduled.
analysis.plain_summary: The Holiday Pay Act would amend the Fair Labor Standards Act, the federal wage law, to require that employees covered by it be paid at least one and a half times their regular rate for hours worked on a federal legal public holiday. It writes the new holiday premium into the same enforcement system as the minimum wage and overtime rules, so workers could recover unpaid holiday pay through the Department of Labor or in court. Today, federal law does not require any premium pay for holiday work, so this would create a new guaranteed benefit for hourly workers who work on those days.
analysis.who_benefits: Hourly workers covered by the Fair Labor Standards Act who end up working on federal holidays — typically retail, food service, hospitality, warehouse, and hospital staff — would earn at least 50% extra for those hours [S2]. Workers shorted on holiday pay could recover the unpaid amounts through the same enforcement machinery as unpaid overtime, including back pay and penalties [S2].
analysis.who_benefits_short: Hourly workers who work federal holidays

how_it_helps.text: Requires covered employers to pay at least one and one-half times the regular rate for work performed on a legal public holiday, a category defined as the federal holidays listed in Title 5 U.S.C. 6103(a) [S2].

Gives the new holiday premium the same enforcement teeth as the minimum wage and overtime rules: unpaid holiday compensation is added to what the Department of Labor and employees can recover under FLSA sections 15, 16, and 17, with a three-year (two-year, extended) limitations period matching unpaid overtime under the Portal-to-Portal Act [S2].

Prevents the federal standard from overriding stronger protections, by providing that the Act excuses noncompliance with no federal, state, or local law that requires higher holiday pay or covers more holidays [S2].
Blocks employers from counting the holiday premium toward the overtime compensation they owe, so a worker's overtime obligation cannot be reduced by holiday-pay payments [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Employers that schedule hourly staff on federal holidays — especially retail chains, restaurants, hospitality, warehouses, and hospitals — would face higher payroll costs on those days. Some may respond by cutting holiday staffing or shifting hours to avoid the premium. Salaried employees exempt from the FLSA's wage and overtime rules, and the narrow industry categories listed in section 13(f), would not receive the holiday premium at all [S2].

drawbacks.text: It raises labor costs for employers operating on federal holidays, such as retailers, restaurants, and hospitals, and some may reduce holiday shifts or scheduling as a result, since the bill does not restrict how employers adjust staffing in response [S2].

It does not help salaried, executive, professional, and administrative workers who are exempt from the FLSA's wage-and-hours rules, nor the industry categories exempted under section 13(f), which the bill adds to the exempted sections — so the holiday premium applies only to already-covered hourly workers [S2].
The bill repeals FLSA section 10 (29 U.S.C. 210) as a conforming change while rewriting the Act's section structure, a deletion whose full scope is not explained in the bill text itself [S2].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The direct benefit is real but targeted: a 50% pay premium on federal holidays for covered hourly workers, enforced like overtime law. The main cost is higher payroll expense for holiday-operating businesses, which may pass some back to workers through reduced holiday shifts. The bill is narrowly drafted, and its coverage gaps mean millions of exempt salaried workers get nothing from it.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, where it currently sits with no committee vote or floor action scheduled [S1][S4].

narrative.text: Sen. Ruben Gallego introduced the bill on February 12, 2026 [S1][S4].
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the same day [S4].
No other senator has cosponsored it as of the latest record, and no committee markup or floor vote has occurred [S3][S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: So far nothing has changed: holiday workers get no new pay, and employers face no new costs. Status quo serves employers with no holiday premium.

for.name: Sen. Ruben Gallego
for.what_they_did: Introduced the Holiday Pay Act and it was referred to the HELP Committee.

sides.party_line_note: The only recorded action is a lone Democratic sponsor with zero cosponsors; no votes have been taken, so no partisan split can be measured yet.

industries.industry: Retail, food service, and hospitality employers
industries.note: These businesses operate heavily on federal holidays and would owe 1.5x pay for hourly staff on those days. The extra pay goes directly into workers' pockets, so the industry's cost is workers' gain.
Hospitals run full schedules on holidays and would face higher premium-pay costs for covered hourly staff. Patients would see no direct change in care.

industries.industry: Exempt salaried professionals and executive, administrative, and professional employees
industries.note: The FLSA's exempt categories are excluded, so salaried workers who already often receive holiday benefits informally get no federal guarantee from this bill.

analysis.trajectory: With a single sponsor, zero cosponsors, and referral to the Senate HELP Committee in the closing year of the 119th Congress, the bill's realistic path is that it never receives a committee vote or floor action and expires at the end of the Congress. Labor bills with bipartisan support occasionally move; this one currently shows none.
